Is it likely that the residents of the uninfested building will prevail in a tort lawsuit against the fumigation company?
A. No, because the HOA owners were responsible for accurately conveying the condition of their buildings.
B. No, because the fumigation company exercised a high degree of caution.
C. Yes, because the fumigation company may be held to a strict liability standard for its activities.
D. Yes, because the fumigation company released a dangerous product into the stream of commerce.

Question: The landlord owns a two-story building. The landlord leased the building and surrounding property to a tenant for a term beginning December 1, 2006, and ending November 30, 2008. Their lease agreement contained the following provision: "Tenant agrees to pay rent at a rate of $500 U.S. dollars per month on or before the first day of each month and to maintain the building located in the leased premises in the same good condition as it was on the date of the lease." On April 15, 2007, the tenant held an annual "Tax Time" party, where she and her friends all went together to the post office to mail their taxes, and then drank and dined at the tenant’s apartment to celebrate. After several drinks, one of the tenant’s friends became confrontational with one of the party guests who challenged the friend’s deductions. The friend lunged at another party participant and crashed into a wall after the other person stepped out of the way. As a result of the incident, one of the walls of the apartment was damaged. This state is a common law jurisdiction. Further, the statute of limitations for a claim to recover damages for negligence is five years from the date the cause of action accrues. In a subsequent suit to interpret the tenant’s obligation under the agreement to keep the premises in repair, which of the following is most accurate?
A. The tenant is responsible for ordinary wear and tear under the repair agreement.
B. The tenant is responsible under such an agreement for all defects, including the damage to the wall.
C. The tenant’s repair agreement is void as against public policy because the landlord is obligated to repair the premises that have deteriorated.
D. The tenant’s obligation to keep the premises in good repair relieves the landlord of the duty to disclose any latent defects.

Question: A woman owned four beach houses. Each house had star-shaped windows. As hurricane season approached, she hired a carpenter to build star-shaped windows and deliver them to the four houses. Due to the unique shape of the windows, the carpenter was forced to do all the work by hand. The carpenter and the woman signed a contract whereby the carpenter promised to build and deliver storm windows to all four beach houses within 30 days, and the woman promised to pay $8,000 ($2,000 per house) within one week after completion of the work. Two weeks after signing the contract, a fire destroyed the carpenter's workshop where he stored all the completed storm windows pending delivery. The carpenter then sent the woman a letter stating: "The fire destroyed my equipment and inventory, including the storm windows that were completed and awaiting delivery. I am ruined and cannot fulfill my contractual obligations." The woman then called the carpenter and told him: "If you do not fulfill your contractual obligations, I will sue you!" In a suit for specific performance to force the carpenter to build and deliver the storm windows, the woman will most likely
A. succeed, because the carpenter's loss of inventory does not excuse his duty to perform.
B. succeed, because the beach houses will suffer serious damage in the event of a hurricane without the installation of storm windows.
C. fail, because the carpenter's performance would be excused by an act of God.
D. fail, because the carpenter's loss of inventory would make his performance impossible.

Question: The owner of a ranch – the owner of a ranch located on top of a mountain. Below the ranch is an estate owned by a millionaire. A stream is a non-navigable waterway that originates on the mountain top and descends into the valley. Both the ranch and the estate are within the watershed of the stream. When the millionaire purchased the estate in 1956, he began taking water from the stream and using it to irrigate the southern half of his property, which he used as a farm. By 1956, the southern half of the estate had been cleared and cultivated, while the northern half remained wooded and virtually unused. The millionaire continued this established pattern of use and never ceased using the water in this manner. In 1986, the ranch owner built a house on the ranch and began drawing water from the stream for domestic purposes. That year there was heavy rainfall, and this resulted in the stream flowing from the mountain at a high water level. However, in 1987, a drought caused a very low water level. Therefore, there was only enough water to irrigate the millionaire’s farmland or, alternatively, to provide all of the ranch owner’s domestic water needs and one-quarter of the millionaire’s irrigation needs. The mountain is located in a jurisdiction where the statute of limitations is 15 years. The ranch owner continues to take water for personal use, but it is not enough to irrigate the estate. Then the millionaire files a proper suit in 1996 to declare that his rights to the water in the stream prevail over the rights of the ranch owner. Furthermore, the millionaire moves to have the full flow of the stream pass to him, notwithstanding the impact this may have on the ranch owner. If this state follows the common law of riparian rights, but does not follow the doctrine of prior appropriation, who should the court rule for?
A. The ranch owner, because as the landowner upstream, he would have greater rights to the water than the landowner downstream.
B. The rancher, because domestic use is superior and protected over agricultural use.
C. The millionaire, because he obtained an easement by prescription to divert as much water as he needs.
D. The millionaire, because he used the water for benefit earlier than the ranch owner, and continuously used the water.

Question: Two cousins inherited real property as joint tenants with right of survivorship. The first cousin pledged his share of the joint tenancy as security for a $20,000 loan and signed a promissory note. Later, this was entered as a judgment against the cousin’s share in the real property. The cousin died a year later. The surviving cousin decided to sell the property, but the mortgagee filed a suit for possession and to compel him to sell. The surviving cousin defended on the ground that any lien on the deceased cousin’s share in the property was extinguished upon the cousin’s death. Will the court enforce the mortgagee’s lien against the sale of the property by the surviving cousin?
A. Yes, because the consent of the cousin to the lien by judgment is presumed by law, and this consent destroyed the joint tenancy.
B. Yes, because a mortgage or judicial lien against one joint tenant destroys the tenancy and destroys the right of survivorship.
C. No, because a joint tenant cannot lawfully subject a judicial judgment solely to the interest of that joint tenant, as that would be an unconstitutional interference with the property rights of the other.
D. No, because when the cousin died, the surviving cousin became the sole owner by virtue of the right of survivorship, pursuant to the joint tenancy, which was wholly unimpaired.

Question: The defendant told two men that a medical equipment company was now using an old warehouse by the river to store defibrillators. One evening, the two men broke into the warehouse and began loading large boxes of defibrillators onto their truck. As they were leaving, one of the men accidentally dropped a cigarette butt into a pile of old cardboard boxes and papers. Shortly thereafter, the trash ignited into a small fire. Although the men could have extinguished the fire without endangering themselves, they did not. Instead, they fled. Meanwhile, the fire quickly spread, engulfing the entire warehouse. If the defendant is later charged with being an accomplice to conspiracy, he is most likely to be held liable
A. as an accessory before the fact.
B. as a second-degree director.
C. as an accomplice.
D. not liable.

Question: In which of the following situations could the defendant's state of intoxication NOT disprove his criminal guilt?
A. The defendant drank one-fifth of bourbon. Later that day, he approached the victim, waving a knife, and told her to go with him, or he would strike her. He led the victim to his car and then ordered her to undress. As the victim was removing her stockings, she kicked the defendant in the head, temporarily stunning him. Then the victim safely fled the car. The defendant was arrested and charged with assault with intent to commit rape.
B. The defendant attended a wedding at a hotel where he drank several vodka daiquiris. After the reception, the defendant began a violent altercation with a parking lot attendant. The defendant retrieved a wheel chock from his car and threw it at the attendant. The wheel chock missed the attendant and struck a passerby as he was entering the hotel. The defendant was arrested and charged with assault with intent to commit battery.
C. The defendant spent the entire evening drinking alcoholic beverages at a bar with three of his friends. An undercover detective overheard the defendant and his friends planning to rob the bar after closing. When the defendant attempted to pull a pistol from his coat, he was quickly disarmed and arrested by detectives. The defendant is charged with robbery.
D. At his law school graduation party, the defendant drank two packs of beer. Around midnight, a girl approached the defendant and asked him for a ride home. Although the girl was only 15 years old, she appeared to be a woman in her early twenties. The defendant, who had been watching the girl all night, quickly agreed and showed her the way to his car. Once inside, they engaged in sexual intercourse. The age of consent in this jurisdiction is 17 for females. The defendant was later arrested and charged with rape.

Question: A player learned that his friend was going on vacation to visit a casino. A gambler, who had been a passionate fan of college football, approached his friend. The player explained that he wanted to place a bet with a bookmaker on his favorite team winning the college football championship next year. He then explained that he had read that his team's chances of winning the football championship next year were listed as 100-1, and he wanted to bet $1000 on his team. The gambler told his friend that he would pay him for his efforts. After further discussion, the gambler wrote the following agreement: "I hereby promise to pay my friend $100 if he places a $1000 bet for me on my favorite team winning the college football championship next year. The bet should be placed at My Lucky Sportsbook in the casino. I also promise to pay my friend $100 US within 30 days after the bet is made. The friend promised not to tell anyone about the bet. After both the player and his friend signed the agreement, the player gave him $1100, that is, $1000 to make the bet, and $100 as an initial fee for the friend's efforts. The friend then went on vacation. Shortly after arriving, the friend tried to place the bet for the player. However, the friend discovered that the player's Lucky Casino had recently closed its sportsbook. The friend then went to another nearby casino and found that they had a sportsbook that also offered 100-1 odds on the player's favorite team winning the college football championship next year. The friend placed the bet with the sportsbook of another casino. Upon returning from vacation, the friend gave the betting slip to the player. Nothing more was said until 30 days later, when the friend asked the player when he would receive the remaining $100. After that, the player refused to pay the friend any more. Which of the following is the best defense for the player in the event of a breach of contract by the friend regarding the receipt of $100?
A. The contract was void ab initio because the contract could not be fully performed within one year.
B. The fact that the friend placed a $1000 bet at a different casino instead of playing at the player's casino constituted a material breach of the contract, releasing the player from any further contractual obligations under the agreement.
C. While on vacation, the friend told his girlfriend about the $1000 he bet on behalf of the player.
D. Because the player's Lucky Casino no longer had a sportsbook to place the bet on, all contractual obligations were suspended under the doctrine of frustration of purpose.

Question: During deer hunting season, open to hunters with firearms, one hunter saw a deer in the forest. He shot his rifle at the deer, hoping to hit and kill it. Instead, he hit and wounded a tourist. The hunter did not realize there was a tourist there. Does the injured traveler have a claim against the hunter for damages?
A. No, because the hunter did not intend to shoot the tourist.
B. No, because the hunter had no direct physical contact with the tourist.
C. Yes, because the bullet from the hunter's rifle made direct physical contact with the tourist.
D. Yes, because the hunter intentionally fired a rifle.

Question: A man and wife were in an unhappy marriage. The man was an alcoholic who physically abused his wife when he became drunk. One night, the man beat his wife, and she decided to kill him. The wife, who had experience with firearms, planned to shoot the man while he slept. Before carrying out her plan, the wife took out a life insurance policy on the man for $1,000,000, naming herself as the beneficiary. Shortly thereafter, the man and wife celebrated their 10th wedding anniversary. They went out to dinner and had a truly pleasant evening together. After a wonderful night, the wife changed her heart and decided that she truly loved her husband and did not want to kill him. The wife confessed and told her husband about her plan, begging for forgiveness. The husband was outraged. He filed for divorce and reported the wife's plan to the police. If the wife is charged with attempted murder, she should be found
A. guilty, because she purchased a life insurance policy.
B. guilty, because she intended to kill her husband.
C. not guilty, because she did not take a substantial action in committing the murder.
D. innocent, because she actually withdrew from the criminal activity.

Question: A woman was seven months pregnant with her first child. One day, the woman was preparing a snack in her home's kitchen when she looked out the window and saw a horrific crime taking place. The woman watched in horror as a member of a local gang pulled out a gun and used it to shoot a victim, a member of a rival gang. The gang member did not know that anyone had witnessed him shooting the victim. The woman watched as the victim collapsed and fell dead on the lawn in front of a neighbor. As a result of the shock from witnessing this horrific event, the woman had a miscarriage. If the woman brings a claim against the local gang member who shot the victim, the woman will
A. recover, because she suffered physical injury, not just emotional.
B. recover, because the gang member acted intentionally, shooting the victim.
C. not recover, because the woman was not in the zone of danger.
D. not recover, because the gang member did not know the woman was watching.

Question: The federal law provides states with funds for child protection programs on the condition that such programs are carried out in accordance with federal standards. The United States filed a lawsuit against the state in federal court seeking an injunction, alleging that the state's child protection programs, partially funded by federal funds allocated under this statute, did not comply with federal standards. The state dismissed the lawsuit. Is it likely that the court will deny the lawsuit?
A. No, because Congress can impose any conditions on the receipt of federal funds.
B. No, because the Eleventh Amendment does not prohibit lawsuits filed by the United States.
C. Yes, because the Eleventh Amendment prohibits lawsuits against a state in federal court.
D. Yes, because the responsibility for child welfare is entrusted to the states.

Question: As a result of a traffic accident involving the defendant, a man and his passenger died. Now, the man's wife is filing a lawsuit for damages for loss of consortium and society. The wife testified that she and her husband had a close relationship and were happily married for over 15 years. Then, during cross-examination, the defendant's lawyer asked her if she "knew about the affair her husband had with his passenger?" The wife's lawyer immediately objected to this question. The judge must rule that the question is
A. subject to objection because the question goes beyond the direct examination.
B. subject to objection because it was unduly prejudicial.
C. not subject to objection because the plaintiff’s knowledge of such a matter was evidence of the significance to be given to her loss.
D. not subject to objection because it relates to the issue of negligence.

Question: While visiting his son, a grandfather tripped over a toy left on the floor by his four-year-old grandson. The grandfather fell and sustained serious injuries. The grandfather regularly visited his son's home and knew that his grandson regularly left toys scattered around the house. The son never warned the grandfather to watch out for the toys. The grandfather sued his son to recover for the bodily injuries he sustained. At the trial, after the presentation of evidence, both the grandfather and the son filed motions for a directed verdict regarding liability. The jurisdiction abolished the family immunity and applies traditional landowner liability rules. What action should the court take?
A. Deny both motions and submit the case to a jury on the issue of negligence.
B. Deny both motions and submit the case to a jury on the issue of strict liability.
C. Grant the grandfather's motion because the son is legally responsible for failing to warn about the danger of leaving toys on the floor.
D. Grant the son's motion because he had no duty to warn that the grandson might leave toys on the floor.

Question: A paper manufacturing company entered into a contract with a construction company to build a new warehouse. The contract stipulated that the construction company would receive payment after the warehouse was completed. The contractor completed the construction, but there were minor deviations from the plans due to the replacement of certain building materials that were not available on the market. The construction company has finished the work and is demanding payment. The paper company refused to pay due to the deviations from the specifications. Is it likely that the construction company will win a breach of contract lawsuit against the paper company?
A. Yes, the company performing the construction work can always recover for work performed.
B. No, the construction company cannot alter the specifications and expect to be paid.
C. No, the construction company is guilty of fraud and misrepresentation.
D. Yes, the construction company substantially performed the contract.

Question: A man and a woman competed in an illegal drag race. Both were exceeding the speed limit, but were very careful. However, when the woman's tire suddenly blew out, she lost control and crashed, injuring a pedestrian. Subsequently, the pedestrian sued the man because the woman had no insurance or assets. Is it likely that the pedestrian will win this lawsuit?
A. No, because the man did not cause bodily harm.
B. No, because the man was driving very carefully.
C. Yes, because the man and woman acted in concert, engaging in a dangerous activity.
D. Yes, because the man was exceeding the speed limit.

Question: The defendant has been charged with murder. The murder occurred on February 1st. At the time the crime was committed, this jurisdiction required a unanimous verdict from all 12 jurors to convict of a crime punishable by death. On November 1st, the state legislature passed a new law requiring a majority of seven out of 12 jurors to convict of a crime punishable by death. The trial of the defendant began on December 1st. He was subsequently found guilty by a vote of eight to four. Following the trial, the defendant's attorney filed a motion to vacate the verdict. Which of the following would be the most substantial constitutional basis for vacating the verdict?
A. Ex post facto clause.
B. Contract Clause.
C. Due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
D. Sixth Amendment right to a fair trial.

Question: A woman owned a 10-acre parcel of farmland in fee simple. The woman agreed to sell the farmland to a man, and each signed a writing stating that the farmland was sold for “...$10,000, receipt of which is acknowledged.” In fact, the man had not yet paid the woman $10,000. On the date set for closing, the woman delivered the deed to the farmland to the man, who gave the woman a check for $10,000. However, several days after the woman deposited the check, she received a notice from her bank that the check had not been paid due to insufficient funds in the man’s account. The woman then sued the man. At trial, the woman is attempting to testify that the man did not actually pay her $10,000, as stated in their writing. The man objects to the woman’s proposed testimony. Should the trial judge sustain the man’s objection?
A. No, because the rule against secondary evidence does not apply to events occurring after the writing was executed.
B. No, because the hearsay rule of inconsistent statement does not operate to exclude evidence demonstrating lack or failure of consideration.
C. Yes, because the writing appears to be a complete integration of the parties’ agreement.
D. Yes, because the doctrine of promissory estoppel will not allow the woman to recant her own signed acknowledgment that she received $10,000.

Question: As part of his defense against a murder charge, the defendant testified that he committed a bank robbery in another state on the day the victim was killed. The testimony is
A. admissible as hearsay.
B. admissible as an admission.
C. inadmissible as a statement against interest.
D. admissible as a then-existing state of mind.

Question: Once late in the afternoon, a woman was hitchhiking when a man picked her up. Shortly thereafter, the man stopped and parked the car in a roadside rest area. They were smoking marijuana when another car skidded and crashed into the man's car. As a result of the collision, the man's car was damaged and the man sustained bodily injuries. The woman was also injured. In fact, the impact caused her to lose consciousness for several minutes. The woman filed a lawsuit against the other driver, seeking damages for his alleged negligence. At trial, the woman testified about her bodily injuries and the other driver's negligence. In defense, the other driver called an attorney who lived next door to the woman. The attorney offered to testify that after the accident, the woman consulted with him regarding her claim and confidentially asked the attorney how she could falsely testify that she had not been smoking marijuana during the accident. Over the objection of the woman’s attorney, the attorney’s testimony is
A. admissible as an admission.
B. admissible as a statement against interest.
C. inadmissible because it violates the woman’s right against self-incrimination.
D. inadmissible because it violates the attorney-client privilege of confidential communication.

Question: A landlord leased a farm building to a tenant for five years. Rent was payable on the first day of each month, and the landlord retained the right to terminate the lease if the tenant failed to perform their obligations. The lease term expired 18 months ago. However, the tenant remained in possession of the building and continued to pay rent on time. The landlord continued to accept the rent. The fair rental value of the building is now significantly higher than what the tenant was paying, and the landlord has recently found a third party who will pay a higher rent. When the tenant paid rent six weeks ago, the landlord accepted the rent but wrote to the tenant stating that she must vacate at the end of the month. The tenant, who is still in possession of the building, informed the landlord that she does not want to move and is willing to pay the current fair rental value. The landlord consulted his attorney for advice on the right of possession. Who should determine who has the right to possession?
A. The landlord, because they properly notified of the termination of the lease.
B. The landlord, because they retained the right of reentry.
C. The tenant, because she stated she is willing to pay the current fair rental value.
D. The tenant, because the landlord did not provide just cause for terminating the lease.

Question: An irrevocable written offer (firm offer) by a merchant to sell goods
A. Must be separately signed if the offeree furnishes a form of agreement containing the offer.
B. Has a duration of three months.
C. Is not transferable.
D. Cannot exceed three months, even if considered.

Question: A company transferred a general warranty deed for a vacant lot to a buyer. According to the deed, the grantee and their successors should proportionally participate in paving the road adjacent to the property. The grantee transferred the property to a married couple via a special warranty deed that did not contain any of the deed’s conditions regarding paving a new road. The buyers did not have an attorney and did not conduct a title search. When the road was completed, the buyers, the married couple, refused to pay the share they were required to pay. The original parcel sellers filed a lawsuit against the couple seeking equitable relief without a jury. The judge ruled that the couple had to pay their share of the paving. Will the appellate court affirm the trial court’s judgment?
A. Yes, it is a covenant that runs with the land, as it was intended to apply to heirs and “successors” of the first buyer.
B. Yes, because the landowner is always responsible for their share of improving any adjacent private roads.
C. No, because the general warranty deed from the original sellers did not extend to the first buyer.
D. No, because the requirement for the paving had to be stated in the deed to the married couple, and it was not.

Question: One company offered to sell several batches of stone for landscape design at a specified price and terms. The recipient of the offer sent the offeror a notification stating, "We have received your offer to sell stone for landscape design on the specified terms of this date." The offeror shipped the goods after receiving this notification. On the day of shipment, the recipient published a form of acceptance with minor changes to the terms. After the goods arrived, the recipient of the offer called the offeror's manager and told him that the company could not currently accept the offer, that he was sending the goods back, and "ignore any documents we have sent." The offeror sued the recipient of the offer for breach of contract. Who will prevail?
A. The offeror will prevail because the publication of acceptance completes the contract between the parties.
B. The recipient of the offer will prevail because he never accepted the offer on the same specified terms.
C. The offeror will prevail because he shipped the goods when he received the first acceptance.
D. The recipient of the offer will prevail because he rejected the offer when he called the offeror's manager.

Question: A college student and a man got into an argument in a bar during a game of pool. The college student allegedly started a fight when he hit the man in the head with a pool cue after the man made a winning shot. In a trial for the college student for assault, the prosecution called a college classmate as a witness. The classmate was not present during the bar fight. The classmate offered to testify that the next day during class he approached the college student and said, "It was wrong of you to start a fight with that man over a pool game," after which the college student bowed his head and walked away. The classmate's testimony is
A. admissible as part of res gestae.
B. admissible as a statement.
C. inadmissible as hearsay, not within any recognized exception.
D. inadmissible as partisan.

Question: A patient at a federal hospital reported that a nurse sexually assaulted her. The man was arrested. During the trial, the prosecution presented evidence that the man had been convicted of two prior charges of sexual assault against two other women, both committed approximately two years ago. The charges and the man's modus operandi in those convictions were almost identical to this case. The defense attorney objected to the evidence on the grounds that its prejudicial effect outweighs its probative value. Based on the Federal Rules of Evidence, what is the court most likely to rule on this issue?
A. The evidence is too prejudicial and should be excluded.
B. The evidence is inadmissible because it is not relevant to the charges and has low probative value.
C. The evidence is admissible because current state policy strongly encourages the arrest and prosecution of sexual predators.
D. The evidence is admissible due to the factual similarity to this charge, which gives the evidence significant probative force.

Question: The defendant is being tried for kidnapping. The victim testified that one of the kidnappers called the other "Spid." The prosecutor calls a prison employee to testify that while the defendant was in prison awaiting trial, other inmates referred to the defendant as "Spid." Are the prison employee's testimonies admissible?
A. No, because it is hearsay and not an exception.
B. No, because it is significantly more prejudicial than probative.
C. Yes, as indirect evidence that the defendant was one of the kidnappers.
D. Yes, to confirm the victim's credibility.

Question: A man and wife were shopping at a local department store when the wife saw a dress she particularly liked. The wife, who weighed over 300 pounds, could not find a large enough size to fit her. She then saw a store clerk and asked if the store had the dress in her size. The clerk looked at the wife and said, "You look like a hippopotamus, and I'm very sorry, but we don't have a hippopotamus-sized dress." Another shopper in the store heard this comment and began to laugh. The wife was very upset and quickly ran out of the store. If the wife sues the department store based on the clerk’s actions, the wife will
A. win, because another customer overheard the statement.
B. win, because the clerk’s behavior was extreme and outrageous.
C. lose, because the clerk was simply expressing an opinion.
D. lose, because the wife suffered only minor harm.

Question: A landlord owned an apartment that he leased to a college graduate for a three-year term, beginning December 1, 2007, at a monthly rent of $1,000 USD, payable on the first of each month. After the college graduate resided in the apartment for six months, on June 1, 2008, he transferred his interest in the premises to a college student. The college student paid rent for two months and then transferred his interest to a sophomore college student. The sophomore college student took possession on August 1, 2008, and paid the rent for August but did not pay rent for the subsequent three months of occupancy. Then, on December 1, 2008, the sophomore college student transferred the premises to a freshman college student, who took possession but did not pay rent to the landlord during his period of occupancy from December 1, 2008, to April 1, 2009. On April 5, 2009, the landlord files a lawsuit against the freshman college student to recover the overdue rent for the premises. The freshman is most likely liable for
A. $8,000.00
B. $7,000.00
C. $5,000.00
D. $4,000.00

Question: A man is accused of murdering his wife. The prosecution claims that on December 17th, the man killed his wife by administering a massive injection of succinylcholine while she was sleeping. Succinylcholine is a drug that anesthesiologists use in small quantities as a muscle relaxant. The prosecution alleges that the lethal dose administered to the wife relaxed her lung muscles so much that she suffocated. Other charges allege that the man's primary motive was to obtain his wife's life insurance policy for $500,000, in which he was the beneficiary. The defense called the doctor who signed the wife's death certificate as their first witness. The defendant's lawyer asked her: "Isn't it true that the cause of death was a heart attack?" The doctor answered negatively and stated that the cause of death was unknown. The man's lawyer called her testimony a recent fabrication and asked her if she had stated in the investigative investigation that the cause of death was a heart attack. The prosecution immediately objected to this question. The judge must decide that this question is
A. subject to objection because a party cannot accuse their own witness.
B. subject to objection because the defendant's lawyer did not lay a proper foundation.
C. not subject to objection because a party can accuse their own witness due to a prior inconsistent statement.
D. not subject to objection because the doctor's testimony at the trial, which took place shortly after the death, would be more reliable.

Question: A landlord has a three-story house. The landlord leased the building and surrounding property to a tenant for a term of six years, commencing December 1, 2003, and ending November 30, 2009. On April 15, 2004, a neighbor who owned an adjacent parcel of land burned leaves and underbrush on his land. A strong wind was blowing in the direction of the land leased to the tenant, and the wind carried the burning leaves onto the tenant’s property. The building caught fire, and the damage from the fire was $150,000. Because of the fire, the tenant has not occupied the leased premises since the date of the fire, as the building was uninhabitable. This state is a common law jurisdiction. Furthermore, the controlling statute of limitations for a cause of action to recover damages for negligence is five years from the date the cause of action accrues. On May 1, 2004, the landlord files a lawsuit against the tenant alleging breach of contract for failure to pay rent. The court should rule
A. for the landlord, because the tenant remains obligated to pay rent even though the property became uninhabitable as a result of the fire.
B. for the landlord, because the obligation to pay rent is tied to the land.
C. for the tenant, because it would be inequitable to enforce a provision in the lease agreement when the premises were rendered uninhabitable.
D. for the tenant, because an increasing number of states have enacted statutes that excuse the tenant from the obligation to pay rent if the premises become uninhabitable due to fire or other acts of God.

Question: A man and a woman, who were friends, decided to jointly purchase a car. The man put in $5,000, and the woman’s father signed a loan for $10,000. The title was registered in the woman’s name, and the man paid the loan. They verbally agreed that it would be joint ownership, equal. After a few months, their relationship deteriorated. They argued over ownership and use of the car. One day, the man tried to drive the car away, but the woman got in and continued to argue while he was driving. He then crashed into a pole and destroyed the car just to spite her, saying that if he couldn’t have it, no one could. Law enforcement arrested the man for car theft (taking a car from its owner) and hooliganism (damaging someone else's or joint property). Assuming that the accuracy of the above facts is beyond a reasonable doubt, which crime or crimes are likely to result in a conviction?
A. He could be convicted of theft, but not of criminal actions.
B. He cannot be convicted of any crime.
C. He can only be convicted of hooliganism.
D. He could be convicted of both theft and hooliganism.

Question: A recent law school graduate was hired by a bar review course on an oral agreement with the editorial consultant. Her duties included preparing new course outlines, proofreading, and grading student homework. The bar review course agreed to pay the graduate an initial salary of $2,500 per month. After three months, the course’s regional director approached the graduate and handed her a newly published 60-page brochure titled “Employee Handbook.” He instructed the graduate to read the handbook and noted that it contained important information regarding the company’s policy considerations and employee compensation. That evening, the graduate returned home and began reading the handbook. After reading approximately 30 pages, the graduate became tired and went to sleep. She never finished reading the rest of the handbook. Six months later, the graduate received a notice of termination from the bar review course. The notice stated that the graduate was being terminated for failure to perform her duties because she complained about the low quality of the bar review course materials and refused to work overtime. After her termination, the graduate filed a lawsuit against the bar review course for breach of contract. What, if proven true, would provide the best defense for the bar review course?
A. All other employees of the bar review course worked overtime when it was required.
B. When the graduate agreed to work for the bar review course, the company never made any promises regarding job security or length of employment.
C. The materials in the bar review course had recently been reviewed by the Committee on Legal Education of the American Bar Association and received a “high rating.”
D. The second page of the bar review course handbook contained a paragraph stating that all policies, instructions, and compensation for employees are “entirely voluntary and not intended to create any continuing contractual obligations.”

Question: A lawsuit arose in a state court when the Secretary of Commerce attempted to prevent a person from mailing their new advertising brochures. According to the Secretary’s interpretation, the new brochures contained obscene pictures and expressions of a sexual nature. The Secretary acted pursuant to authority granted to him by section 1123(b) of the state statute, which provided: “If the Secretary of Commerce determines that a commercial mailing to residents of the state is patently offensive to minors, the Secretary has the power to prohibit such mailing.” The case reached the highest state court, which held the statute unconstitutional because it violated both commerce clause and anti-commandeering provisions. If the case is reviewed by the U.S. Supreme Court, it will reach that court
A. by filing a petition.
B. by certiorari.
C. if five justices vote to review it.
D. notwithstanding the doctrine of adequate and independent state grounds.

Question: The suspect was arrested and charged with conspiracy to obtain stolen property. A defense attorney represented the defendant during arraignment. After posting bail, he was released. After his release, the defendant again found work as a bartender at a local bar. Three weeks before the scheduled trial of the defendant, an informant entered the bar. After several drinks, the informant began a conversation with the defendant, who was on duty at the time. The defendant did not know that the man was a paid police informant. During their conversation, the informant told the defendant that he had read about his arrest in the newspapers and asked the defendant the names of his accomplices. Unsuspecting, the defendant made some admissions, which the informant then relayed to the prosecutor. At trial, the prosecution sought to introduce the defendant's admissions into evidence. The defendant's motion to exclude this offer of evidence will most likely be
A. denied, as the defendant’s statements were voluntary.
B. overruled, as the defendant assumed the risk that his trust in the informant was misplaced.
C. granted, as the defendant’s right to counsel under the Sixth Amendment was violated.
D. granted, as the defendant’s right against self-incrimination under the Fifth Amendment was violated.

Question: The defendant decided to rob a bar because he knew the bar was now using a new security system that was faulty, and that the night was the best time to break in. Late in the evening, the defendant broke into the bar and began loading large barrels of beer onto his truck. As he was leaving, the defendant inadvertently threw a cigarette butt into a trash can behind the bar. Shortly thereafter, the trash caught fire in a small blaze. Although the defendant could have extinguished the fire without any danger to himself, he did not. Instead, he got into his truck and drove off. Although the fire spread beyond the trash can, firefighters quickly responded and were able to extinguish it. The floor behind the bar is charred. Statutes for both burglary and arson in this jurisdiction include residential and business structures. For which of the following crimes should the defendant be convicted?
A. Arson, burglary, and theft.
B. Arson and robbery.
C. Theft and robbery.
D. Arson, robbery, and burglary.

Question: In a large city, garbage is always a problem. The state's law on combating garbage prohibits throwing garbage and other items from any vehicle onto public roads. This is an administrative offense, which involves a fine of $50 without imprisonment. For a third offense, the fine is $500 and imprisonment for 5 days is provided. The statute contains no requirement of criminal intent. John and his family are returning from a weekend picnic when his children throw garbage bags and leftover dinner out the back window of a moving car. John is stopped and given a $50 ticket. Can he succeed in defending himself by claiming that he did not know what his children were doing and that he had no criminal intent to violate any laws?
A. No, because this is likely a strict liability law, which does not allow a defense based on mental state.
B. Yes, because he did not know what his children were doing in the back seat, and he did not participate in the violation and did not know that they were doing it or intended to do it.
C. Yes, because the police cannot prove who threw the garbage out the window in the car.
D. No, because his criminal intent is clearly established by the circumstances of the event.

Question: At a subway station in the city, significant construction is always underway, including the reconstruction of a lift shaft between the platform and ground level. There is a warning sign stating "this lift is currently out of service, please do not use it." A passenger sees the signs but still attempts to ride the lift and is injured when she falls into the shaft. When the passenger sues the city for negligence, the city claims she assumed the risk. Is this a valid and accurate defense under these circumstances?
A. Yes, because she was fully informed and should have known the lift was dangerous based on the signs.
B. Yes, because the signs indicate her negligence and are a lawful reason for her own harm.
C. No, because the sign did not explain the danger, but only stated that it was out of service, and therefore she did not know what she was facing.
D. No, because the city has strict liability when everyone depends on the subway.

Question: Daylight Corp. manufactured, assembled, and sold a steel cutting press designed to cut aluminum sheets into can lids. In 2002, Goodboy Beverages purchased a deluxe model of Daylight’s cutting press for $20,000. In 2002 and 2003, Daylight received several complaints about dangerous malfunctions of other cutting presses. In response, Daylight created a safety device and offered it for $5,000 in a brochure sent to all of its customers, noting that several users had been injured while using the cutting press model. Goodboy received the brochure but did not purchase the $5,000 safety device. In 2004, a Goodboy employee was injured by the press. During the litigation, Daylight argued that if Goodboy had purchased the safety device, the injury would not have occurred, and sought a directed verdict. The court should
A. Grant Daylight’s motion because Goodboy’s refusal to purchase the safety device was an assumption of risk.
B. Deny the motion because Goodboy’s negligence in failing to purchase the safety device was less than Daylight’s negligence in initially manufacturing a dangerous press.
C. Deny the motion because the jury may find that Daylight could not reasonably have foreseen that Goodboy would not want to pay $5,000 for a safety device.
D. Deny the motion because the press was inherently dangerous, Daylight owed strict liability.

Question: A man who owned a haberdashery made an order by telephone to a wholesale supplier of cashmere and wool clothing for "three dozen purple cashmere socks, size 1013 at the current resale price." The supplier's sales agent orally accepted the order at the agreed price of $250 per dozen. In accordance with the supplier's usual business practice, the sales agent mailed a confirmation letter, which he signed and dated: "According to your telephone order, this letter serves to confirm the purchase of 36 dozens of cashmere socks, color purple, size 10. 13, at the agreed price of $250 USD per dozen: $9,000 USD. This letter was received by the man, who glanced at it casually but did not notice the notation "36 dozens." The man placed the letter in his papers and did not respond to it. Three weeks later, the supplier tendered 36 dozens of purple cashmere socks, which the man rejected on the grounds that he had ordered only three dozens. The supplier resold the same purple cashmere socks to another buyer for a total price of $8,000. The supplier sued the man for the difference of $1,000. If the man relies on fraud as a defense, will such a defense be successful?
A. Yes, because the statute was not satisfied by the tender of the goods by the supplier, which were rejected by the man, and the supplier did not rely on the oral agreement except to attempt delivery.
B. Yes, because the agreed price for three dozens of socks was over $500, and the supplier's memorandum incorrectly stated the quantity of goods ordered.
C. No, because the written memorandum of the supplier was sufficient to satisfy the requirements of the statute against the supplier, and the man, having grounds to know the contents of the memorandum, failed to give notice of dissent within 10 days after receipt.
D. No, because the supplier's written memorandum acted as an acceptance, with additional terms that became part of the contract after the man failed to object to such additional terms within a reasonable time.

Question: Anticipating an increase in business during the holiday season, a retail store owner decided to hire an additional employee. On October 31st, the owner entered into a written contract with the employee, stipulating that the employee would be employed at the retail store in November and December for $2,000 per month. At the end of November, the owner noticed that the business had not grown as much as he had expected. The owner informed the employee that if he did not agree to a salary reduction, he would be terminated. Reluctantly, on December 1st, the employee verbally agreed to a $500 reduction in salary for December. Which of the following statements regarding the December 1st agreement between the owner and the employee is most accurate?
A. It effectuated a valid reformation of their initial written agreement.
B. It effectuated a valid modification of their initial written contract.
C. It effectuated a novation of their initial written contract.
D. It did not alter the rights and obligations of the parties pursuant to the terms of their original contract.

Question: A 55-year-old man presented to the doctor with recurrent widespread blistering over 2 weeks. Physical examination shows lesions, most numerous in flexural areas, including the axillary folds and groin. The blisters do not easily rupture, and there are no oral mucosal lesions. These blisters are most likely the result of an adhesion defect involving which of the following?
A. Basement membrane
B. Dermal papillae
C. Langerhans cells
D. Melanocytes

Question: One Sunday, a sports fan went to a professional soccer match. Standing in line at a kiosk, he argued with three men who were standing ahead in line. The three men were friends and were attending the game together. One of the men punched the fan in the mouth. A fight broke out. During the altercation, one of the other three men hit the fan in the head with a bottle, causing him to suffer a serious concussion. The sports fan is certain he does not know which of the three men hit him with the bottle. If the sports fan sues the man who punched him in the mouth to recover damages for the head injury, will the sports fan prevail?
A. Yes, because the man who punched him in the mouth was the instigator who delivered the first blow, which started the fight.
B. Yes, because the man who punched him in the mouth and the other men acted in concert.
C. No, because the man who punched him in the mouth did not actually hit the sports fan with the bottle.
D. No, because the sports fan cannot provide proof as to which of the men hit him in the head with the bottle.

Question: A married couple sued a real estate broker for misrepresentation and breach of contract due to the broker's failure to fulfill promises made regarding the purchase of a home. They claimed they received promises from the broker that if they immediately purchased the house, the sellers would provide them with a $15,000 discount after closing. At closing, the sellers claimed they were unaware of and did not provide the discount. During the lawsuit against the broker, the couple called one of the broker's agents to court, who testified that he was at the meeting with the buyers and heard the broker make the same promise. The broker objected that the testimony was hearsay. What is the court most likely to rule regarding the admissibility of the testimony?
A. The testimony is admissible because it is an admission by a party made through an authorized agent of the party regarding a matter within the agent’s scope of employment.
B. The testimony is inadmissible because the agent was not authorized to act on behalf of his principal.
C. The testimony is inadmissible because it is classic hearsay offered to prove the truth of a disputed matter.
D. The testimony is admissible even if it is hearsay, as the broker is available for cross-examination.

Question: Once late in the evening, an accountant went into a bar and ordered sour whiskey. The bartender served the drink, although the accountant looked and behaved as if he was already very drunk. The accountant soon drank five more cocktails, which the bartender served despite the fact that the accountant was clearly and unmistakably drunk. After finishing his sixth drink at the bar, the accountant wished the bartender good night, swayed, left the bar, got into a car, and drove off. Driving several blocks weaving back and forth on the road, the accountant crashed his car into a pedestrian walking on the sidewalk next to the road. The pedestrian sustained serious injuries to his back and legs. The bartender's actions in serving drinks to the accountant are most likely to be considered as
A. the proximate cause of the pedestrian's injuries.
B. a contributing cause of the pedestrian's injuries.
C. the direct cause of the pedestrian's injuries.
D. an intervening cause of the pedestrian's injuries.

Question: A healthy 2-year-old girl was brought to the office for a routine check-up. The child was weaned from breastfeeding at 6 months of age and began walking at 10 months of age. On physical examination, she has mild bowing of the legs (10th degree genu varum). What of the following is most appropriate to recommend guidance at this time?
A. Increased vitamin D intake
B. A special exercise program
C. Surgical correction
D. No treatment is needed at this time

Question: A land development company owned a parcel of land consisting of 400 acres in the Great Lakes area. Over time, the land development company developed two residential portions of the land, an east and west plat, each containing 150 acres. These plats were created by separate deeds which did not refer to each other. However, the restrictions in the deeds were practically identical. The plats and each document provide that “the use of the land conveyed herein is limited to single-family dwellings, and this agreement is intended to apply to each lot in the plat and runs with the land, binding each lot owner, his heirs and assigns.” After all but four lots in each plat had been sold by the land development company, it sold 50 acres of the remaining 100 acres of land to a country club by a deed containing the following provisions: “This deed is entered into and accepted with the understanding that the above-described property is hereby limited so that (1) the property may be used as a country club with a golf course, swimming pool, tennis courts, clubhouse, food service facilities and other appropriate country club improvements (2) the property may also be subdivided and platted as a residential subdivision similar to the east plat, and after such subdivision, the property shall be used and conveyed subject to residential restrictions which conform to the restrictions now against the east plat. (3) the restrictions set forth in this instrument shall be deemed to be covenants running with the land, and for any breach of any covenant in this instrument, the party or parties granting the right – the land development company, its successors and assigns – may, at their election, re-enter and terminate the estate granted by this deed.” At the time of this conveyance, the land company retained ownership of the remaining 50 acres in the original 400-acre tract. Which of the following best describes the country club’s interest in the 50-acre tract it purchased from the land development company?
A. Easement easily determined.
B. Easement conditional upon subsequent events.
C. Covenant to be performed.
D. Subsidiary servitude.

Question: In a 68-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer that has recurred twice in the last 5 years. She has undergone radiation and chemotherapy for metastatic cancer to the bone. Today she comes to the office to ask for help in dealing with back pain in the mid-thoracic region so that she can use less pain medication. The most appropriate osteopathic manipulative technique for treating this patient's spine is
A. high velocity, low amplitude
B. indirect myofascial release
C. isotonic exercise
D. medium velocity, medium amplitude

Question: A 36-year-old female advertising department manager is sent to the office for a fasting serum total cholesterol assessment of 249 mg/dL. She has a family history of early ischemic heart disease (IHD), and her father suddenly died at age 46 from myocardial infarction. She states she has never experienced chest pain. She is currently not sexually active and has no children. She claims that due to a stressful lifestyle, she cannot eat properly or adhere to a special diet, and typically eats fast food. She exercises two to three times per week for approximately 20 minutes on a treadmill. For the past 20 years, she has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily. Her only medication is acetaminophen for tension headaches. Her height is 165 cm (5 feet 5 inches) and her weight is 76 kg (167 pounds); BMI is 28 kg/m2. Vital signs are normal today. Physical examination reveals no abnormalities except for mild obesity. What of the following is the most important step in preventing IHD in this patient?
A. Biofeedback-based stress reduction program
B. A more rigorous and consistent exercise program
C. Smoking cessation program
D. Strict low-calorie diet

Question: A 27-year-old male was admitted to the hospital 45 minutes after being involved in a traffic accident. Physical examination reveals a sluggish response to stimuli. Neurological examination shows no other abnormalities. X-ray of the skull shows a linear fracture of the base of the skull without depression. Two weeks later, the patient develops polyuria and polydipsia. Laboratory tests show a normal serum glucose concentration, elevated serum osmolality, and decreased urine osmolality. After desmopressin administration, urine osmolality increases. The beneficial effect of this drug is most likely due to activation of which of the following?
A. Adenylyl cyclase
B. Ca2+ channels
C. Janus kinase
D. Serine kinase

Question: A 44-year-old woman presents to the clinic for evaluation of a neck mass she noticed 1 week ago. She denies any tenderness, fever, weight loss, or fatigue. Physical examination reveals a freely mobile 2 cm mass in the lower left lobe of the thyroid gland. In addition to thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine levels, the most appropriate initial diagnostic modality for this lesion is
A. thyroid gland nuclear scan
B. iodine-131 scan
C. fine-needle aspiration
D. thyroid gland ultrasound

Question: A 37-year-old male presented to the emergency department complaining of nausea and dizziness for the past hour. He has a significant history of esophageal varices secondary to alcoholic cirrhosis of the liver and ascites, which are treated with spironolactone. He consumes eight to ten alcoholic beverages daily. While you are obtaining additional history, the patient vomits a large amount of bright red blood, and he is difficult to arouse. Vital signs: temperature 36.0°C (96.8°F), pulse 110/min, respirations 12/min, and blood pressure 90/50 mmHg. After initiating intravenous fluid resuscitation, which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
A. Arrange for transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt
B. Initiate intravenous vasopressin therapy
C. Perform endotracheal intubation
D. Perform upper endoscopy

Question: A 27-year-old woman presented to the doctor complaining of chronic diarrhea for 3 years and periodic cramping pain in the lower abdomen. The pain usually subsides during defecation and does not occur at night or interfere with sleep. She says she is frustrated with her symptoms and has stopped traveling due to frequent, urgent need to use the toilet. She has no serious illnesses and is not taking any medications. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse 70/min, respiration 14/min, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. The lower abdomen is slightly tender on palpation; there is no rebound tenderness or guarding. The rest of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory test results are within reference ranges. Fecal occult blood test is negative. Anti-gliadin antibodies are absent. What of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
A. Nefazodone
B. Nortriptyline
C. Phenelzine
D. Sertraline

Question: A 27-year-old woman, pregnancy 2, para 1, presents for a prenatal visit at 12 weeks gestation. She feels well. Her first pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. Medications include folic acid and a multivitamin. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), blood pressure is 108/60 mmHg. Pelvic examination reveals a uterus that is consistent with a 12-week gestation. Urine dipstick shows leukocyte esterase; urinalysis shows leukocytes and few gram-negative rods. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A. Recommend drinking 8 ounces of cranberry juice daily
B. Oral therapy with amoxicillin
C. Oral therapy with metronidazole
D. Intravenous therapy with cefazolin

Question: A 40-year-old man presented to the clinic with symptoms of odynophagia and gastroesophageal reflux. He also states that he had vomiting last week. His past medical history reveals HIV, and his most recent CD4 level was 30 cells/µL. Tilt test and hemoglobin levels are normal. Rectal examination reveals brown stool that is positive for occult blood. What is the most appropriate initial step in managing this patient?
A. prescription for a proton pump inhibitor and prokinetic
B. prescription for a trial of an H2-blocker for 6 weeks
C. prescription for clotrimazole tablets
D. referral for upper endoscopy with biopsy

Question: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the office for a routine check-up. She was diagnosed with Turner syndrome in childhood during an examination for aortic coarctation. During today's visit, her mother reports that the girl has been talking about babies. You have been the patient's doctor for the past 6 years and know that she is in a pre-pubertal state. It would be most appropriate to advise the patient that if she wants to have a family, she needs to do what of the following?
A. Adopt
B. Have an amniocentesis if she becomes pregnant
C. Have surgery
D. Obtain genetic counseling

Question: A 5-year-old boy was brought to the doctor with a 2-day history of fever and painful swelling of the left ankle. Since childhood, he has suffered from recurrent cervical lymphadenitis and pneumonia. Two years ago, a culture from a neck abscess grew Staphylococcus aureus. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F). Examination shows a tender, erythematous, swollen left ankle; point tenderness over the medial malleolus. Bone scan shows increased uptake in the left lower tibial metaphysis. Culture of bone aspirate grows Serratia marcescens. Nitroblue tetrazolium test shows no color change. What of the following is the most likely mechanism for these findings?
A. Arrest of B-lymphocyte maturation
B. Dysmorphogenesis of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches
C. Chemotaxis defect
D. Defect in phagocytic oxidative metabolism

Question: A 37-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is hospitalized due to inadequate glucose control over the past 2 months. Despite the poor control, he demands to be discharged. He reports fatigue, irritability, and a sense of hopelessness for the past 3 months. He admits to not adhering to his diabetes regimen, adding, "Sometimes I forget." He avoids his family and friends because he doesn't feel like seeing them, but acknowledges that he is lonely. He has been unable to get out of bed for 2 days, prompting his wife to call an ambulance and hospitalize him. Prior to admission, his only medication was insulin, although he frequently missed doses. He denies alcohol use. His height is 168 cm (5 feet 6 inches) and weight is 100 kg (220 pounds); BMI is 36 kg/m2. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 68/min, respiration is 18/min, and blood pressure is 150/85 mmHg. Physical examination reveals no abnormalities. Mental status examination reveals he is fatigued and has a blunted affect. There is no evidence of suicidal ideation. Cognition is intact. His fasting serum glucose is 120 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A. Honor the patient's wishes and discuss home care options
B. Honor the patient's wishes contingent on his agreement to care
C. Order neuropsychological testing
D. Seek a court order for the appointment of a legal guardian

Question: A 26-year-old woman with HIV infection presented to the clinic with pain and redness of the left lower leg for 4 days. She states that the symptoms appeared after she tripped over a tree branch in her yard and scratched her left leg. Current medications include antiretroviral therapy and ibuprofen as needed. Vital signs: temperature 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse 86/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 138/70 mmHg. On the anterior aspect of the left lower extremity, there is a 5 × 8 cm area that is swollen, erythematous, and painful. She previously had a rash after taking erythromycin, and she had an anaphylactic reaction to penicillin. Which of the following antibiotic regimens would be most appropriate for this patient?
A. Amoxicillin
B. Ciprofloxacin
C. Clarithromycin
D. Clindamycin

Question: In 1993, a farmer had a good ownership right to the farm in absolute form. In 1994, the farmer transferred to his son for $1,000 a document signed by the farmer, in which the son and his heirs were named as the subject of the right and appeared valid. The son disregarded the recording of the deed. In 1998, an investor who knew about the existence of the ownership agreement from the farmer to the son found the farmer and asked to buy for $10,000 a deed of ownership of the farm from the farmer to the investor and his heirs. The farmer drew up such a deed, and the investor promptly recorded it. The investor's intention was to acquire the color of title and obtain ownership of the farm through adverse possession. In 1998, the investor built a fence around the farm. In 1999, the son gave his deed to the farm to the ranch owner and, for $15,000 paid by the ranch owner, signed and transferred the deed of the farm to the ranch owner and his heirs. Upon receiving the document, the ranch owner made no effort to verify the title, inspect the property, or record the document. In 2003, the teacher paid the investor $20,000, and the investor transferred the deed of ownership of the farm to the teacher for the benefit of the teacher and his heirs. The teacher inspected the property, verified the title, and knew about the prior instrument from the farmer to the son. Although the teacher did not live on the premises, he regularly visited the farm twice a week. The teacher recorded his act. In 2007, for $25,000 paid by the professor, the ranch owner signed and provided the farm deed, in which the professor and his heirs were named as subsidiarities. Before the professor paid the ranch owner and took the document, the professor visited the farm and inspected the fence. However, the teacher was not present when the professor visited the property, and nothing indicated who was "who" was using it. In any case, the professor did not attempt to search the title before making the purchase. Then the professor recorded the deed. Note. In this jurisdiction, "grantor-grantee" indices are used and there is no treatise index. The jurisdiction's recording statute provides: "Any transfer of real property that is not recorded is invalid as to a subsequent bona fide purchaser for valuable consideration, the transfer of which must initially be properly recorded." In 2008, in a lawsuit over ownership of the farm, which of the following parties would have priority of ownership?
A. Professor.
B. Investor.
C. Teacher.
D. Ranch owner.

Question: A previously healthy 19-year-old college student comes to the student health service 24 hours after the onset of headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. She recalls no contact with sick individuals. She had chickenpox at age 7. Her last examination 1 year ago included a PPD skin test and was unremarkable. She takes a multivitamin and a herbal weight loss supplement daily. She received all appropriate childhood vaccinations but has not had any vaccinations since. She does not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. There is no significant family history. She appears lethargic. Her temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F), pulse 112/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 100/68 mmHg. Diffuse petechiae are noted on examination. Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are present. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable. A lumbar puncture is performed. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis shows numerous segmented neutrophils and a decreased glucose concentration. Gram stain of the CSF reveals gram-negative cocci. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
A. Ceftriaxone
B. Clindamycin
C. Erythromycin
D. Metronidazole

Question: A 67-year-old woman presents to the doctor with mild bruising over the past 4 months. In her history, she had lung cancer that underwent radiation therapy 6 months ago. She has a 2-year history of hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic and an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. Examination, including neurological examination, reveals no abnormalities except for numerous ecchymoses. Hemoglobin concentration is 13 g/dL, leukocytes 5000/mm3, platelets 35,000/mm3. Serum antiplatelet antibody testing is negative. What of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
A. CT of the abdomen
B. CT of the chest
C. Bronchoscopy
D. Bone marrow aspiration

Question: A previously healthy 17-year-old girl presented to the doctor with a cough triggered by physical exertion and nasal congestion for 2 months. She plays field hockey and has noticed that she coughs when running on the field. The cough is non-productive and resolves with rest. She has no chest pain or palpitations. She takes no medications and does not smoke. Her sister has asthma. The patient appears well. Pulse 68/min, respiration 16/min, blood pressure 100/75 mmHg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows oxygen saturation of 99%. Cardiovascular and pulmonary examination reveals no abnormalities. Chest X-ray reveals no abnormalities. Spirometry shows an FEV1:FVC ratio of 90% and FEV1 90% of predicted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. asthma
B. Chronic bronchitis
C. Gastroesophageal reflux disease
D. Postnasal drip syndrome

Question: A 35-year-old man visits the clinic for his HIV test results and is informed that the result is positive. The patient resists disclosing this to his wife, as he has not told her about his extramarital sexual partners. The doctor informs the patient that his wife’s right to know takes precedence, as she may also be HIV-positive. Which of the following relationships best describes the justification for the doctor’s recommendation that the patient inform his wife about his condition rather than conceal this information?
A. autonomy outweighs beneficence
B. autonomy outweighs justice
C. beneficence outweighs autonomy
D. non-maleficence outweighs autonomy

Question: After a severe beating and gunshot wound to the abdomen, a 42-year-old woman undergoes resection of a small bowel perforation. During the operation, plastic reconstruction of facial bone fractures and open reduction and internal fixation of the left femoral bone are also performed. Thirty-six hours postoperatively, she is not sleeping but is not fully alert. She is receiving intravenous morphine via a patient-controlled pump. She states that she needs morphine to relieve pain but is worried about becoming dependent. She has no history of psychoactive disorders. She drinks one to two glasses of wine per week. Which of the following initial actions by the physician is most appropriate?
A. Reassure the patient that her chances of becoming dependent on narcotics are minimal
B. Continue morphine but periodically administer intravenous naloxone
C. Transition the patient to oral acetaminophen as soon as she is able to take oral medications
D. Switch the patient to intramuscular lorazepam

Question: A 27-year-old male was brought to the emergency department by his sister due to progressively worsening altered mental status over 10 hours. He is unable to answer questions. His sister states that he recently saw a psychiatrist for the first time due to hearing voices; he was prescribed medication, but she is unsure what it was. She says he has a history of excessive alcohol use, and she thinks he has also experimented with illicit drugs. He appears acutely ill. His temperature is 39.1°C (102.3°F), pulse 124/min, blood pressure 160/102 mmHg. Examination reveals profuse sweating and muscle rigidity. His neck is stiff. Abdomen is soft, non-tender. Mental status examination reveals psychomotor agitation alternating with lethargy. White blood cell count is 15,600/mm3, serum creatine kinase activity is 943 U/L. What is the most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms?
A. Amphetamine intoxication
B. Bacterial meningitis
C. Delirium tremens
D. Malignant neuroleptic syndrome

Question: A 78-year-old woman is hospitalized for left knee replacement due to degenerative joint disease. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus, a long history of hypertension, and chronic kidney disease, which is secondary to diabetes and hypertension. Reversible causes of kidney failure have been ruled out. She had a tonsillectomy at age 9 and a laparoscopic cholecystectomy at age 68. Her serum creatinine concentration on admission was 6.0 mg/dL. Her current therapy includes an American Diabetes Association (ADA) low-sodium and low-protein diet, enalapril, and acetaminophen. She is a retired seamstress. She and her husband live on a farm 90 miles from the nearest dialysis facility. Considering long-term treatment options for this patient, which of the following factors is most appropriate to consider?
A. Her eligibility for Medicare
B. Her history of abdominal surgery
C. Her history of arthritis
D. Her suitability for home dialysis

Question: A 10-year-old boy was brought in for follow-up 2 days after being seen in the emergency department for urticaria, hoarseness, and dizziness. His symptoms began 15 minutes after being stung by a bee and lasted approximately 60 minutes; they resolved before he was treated. He has been stung by bees three times in the past year, and each reaction has been more severe. Examination reveals no abnormalities. What of the following is the most appropriate recommendation to prevent future morbidity and mortality from this condition?
A. Avoid areas where bees are known to be present
B. Avoid wearing colored clothing outdoors
C. Carrying dimenhydrinate tablets
D. Carrying self-injectable epinephrine

Question: A 77-year-old woman presents to the clinic for evaluation of a syncopal episode that occurred during ambulation. Cardiac examination reveals a 3/6 systolic murmur best heard at the right upper sternal border. Radiation of the murmur to the neck is noted. Which valvular abnormality is most likely to have caused this episode?
A. aortic regurgitation
B. aortic stenosis
C. mitral regurgitation
D. mitral stenosis

Question: A 46-year-old man with Marfan syndrome, aortic insufficiency, and mitral regurgitation presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain for the past 3 hours. He describes the pain as tearing, radiating to the neck. A week prior, he experienced a similar, but less severe, chest pain and took aspirin himself. What of the following is the most likely cause of the worsening symptoms?
A. Acute bacterial endocarditis
B. Acute myocardial infarction
C. Aortic dissection
D. Esophageal reflux with spasm

Question: A 35-year-old man presents for follow-up regarding sarcoidosis. His only new complaint is leg pain that worsens with exertion. He has been taking glucocorticoids for the past 6 months. Vital signs are currently: temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse 78/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. The patient is thin, and denies any acute distress. Auscultation of the chest reveals scattered bilateral basilar crackles. There is mild pain in the left thigh, present with both active and passive range of motion. Dorsalis pedis pulse is intact. Neurological examination is normal. What of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
A. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
B. Disc herniation
C. Hip joint stenosis
D. Osteoporosis

Question: A 46-year-old female, gravida 1, para 1, presented for an appointment complaining of 2-week history of black discharge from the right nipple, which has been ongoing for 2 weeks. The patient had a mammogram and breast ultrasound 2 months ago to evaluate palpable increased density in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, which was detected during the last annual examination. The studies showed likely benign results with recommended follow-up in 6 months. Otherwise, unremarkable medical history, the patient is not taking any medications. BMI is 30 kg/m2. Vital signs are normal. Palpation of the right breast reveals a mass in the upper outer quadrant, but no other formations are present. There is minimal black discharge from the right nipple. What is the most appropriate next step in the diagnostic evaluation?
A. Ductography
B. Excisional biopsy of the glandular tissue
C. Repeat mammography
D. Repeat ultrasound of the right breast

Question: Over 1 year, a study is conducted to assess the anti-leukemic activity of a new tyrosine kinase inhibitor in patients with chronic myeloid leukemia in blast crisis. All patients participating in the study are informed that they will be treated with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor. They are assigned to sequential cohorts of doses ranging from 300 to 1000 mg/day of the drug. Each dose is assigned to six to eight patients. Treatment efficacy is determined based on the results of a complete blood count and bone marrow assessment, which are regularly performed throughout the study. This study is best described as which of the following?
A. Case-control
B. Cross-over study
C. Open-label clinical trial
D. Randomized clinical trial

Question: A 25-year-old woman presented to the doctor with numbness in her right arm for 2 months. During this period, she most often felt tingling in the ring and little fingers of her right hand. She has no serious illnesses and is not taking any medications. She works as a cashier and uses a computer at home. She played pitcher in a softball league for 5 years, until she stopped 2 years ago. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows full muscle strength. Palpation of the right elbow causes sharp pain in the ring and little fingers of the right hand. Sensation of pinprick and light touch is reduced on the medial half of the ring finger of the right hand and on the entire little finger. The most likely cause of these findings is entrapment of which of the following on the right?
A. Median nerve at the wrist
B. Cutaneous nerve in the forearm
C. Radial nerve in the forearm
D. Ulnar nerve at the elbow joint

Question: A 37-year-old woman with AIDS presented to the doctor with a 1-month history of progressive diarrhea and weight loss of 1.8 kg (4 pounds). Over the past week, she has had six large, watery stools daily. She is currently on triple antiretroviral therapy. She is employed as a flight attendant and regularly works on domestic flights within the United States. She also flies to Asia at least once a month. Her height is 163 cm (5 feet 4 inches) and her weight is 59 kg (130 pounds); BMI is 22 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 112/64 mmHg. Her abdomen is boat-shaped. The rest of the examination is unremarkable. Her CD4+ T lymphocyte count is 400/mm3 (normal ≥500). Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?
A. Cryptosporidium parvum
B. Cytomegalovirus
C. Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex
D. Salmonella enteritidis

Question: A 29-year-old man presented to the clinic complaining of palpitations, poor sleep, and a general feeling of restlessness. He moved 2 months ago for a promotion and has found that he cannot concentrate on his new responsibilities. He is worried about his ability to adapt to the increased responsibility at work and states that he has been sick for 3 days over the past 2 weeks. The most likely diagnosis is
A. Adjustment disorder with anxious mood
B. Generalized anxiety disorder
C. Major depressive disorder, single episode, moderate
D. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
